opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and honestly it's mostly a pragmatic decision. When you're building a new modality, there are a lot of things you need to figure out on their own first: the right audio encoder, how you tokenize or represent speech, what data mix works, how you evaluate it. If you try to do all of that inside your main flagship model from day one, every experiment becomes very expensive and very slow, and it's hard to tell what's actually helping.

So what we did is develop the audio side as its own track, with smaller models where we can iterate quickly. Something like transcription and speech understanding is a well-defined problem with clear benchmarks, so you can make fast progress and really know where you stand. And it's also immediately useful: a lot of customers just want very good, cheap, reliable transcription or audio understanding, and they don't necessarily need it bundled into the largest model.

Then once the recipe is mature, once we know the encoder works, we understand the data, and we've solved the training stability issues, merging it into the main models is much less risky. You're not jeopardizing text performance or reasoning, which is still the core of what people use, because you already know how audio behaves. It's the same approach we took with vision: get it right in isolation, then bring it together. Long-term the goal is clearly one model that handles everything natively, but getting there step by step is much more efficient than trying to do everything at once.

r001.rationale: The response says Mistral develops audio as a separate track to iterate quickly on the encoder, speech representation, data mix, and evaluation, then merges it into the main models once the recipe is mature.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it comes down to a few practical things. When you train a speech model separately, you can iterate much faster. The data pipeline for audio is completely different from text: you have to deal with transcription quality, noise, different languages, accents, sampling rates. If you try to do all of that inside the main pretraining run of a large language model, every mistake becomes very expensive. You find out something is wrong with your audio tokenization after three weeks of training, and that's a disaster. Whereas if the audio team can train smaller models on their own, they can ablate things, test different encoders, test different codecs, and get to something that works well before we ever touch the big model.

The second reason is that the text model is the foundation. Most of the reasoning capability, the knowledge, the instruction following comes from text. We don't want to degrade that. So the approach that makes sense to us is: get a very strong language model, get a very strong audio encoder, and then figure out the best way to connect them. Sometimes that's a projection layer and some adaptation training, sometimes it's more involved. But you're starting from two things that already work, rather than hoping that joint training from scratch will make both of them good at the same time, which in our experience it often doesn't.

And there's a third thing, which is simply that it's a different team with different expertise. People who have spent years on speech recognition and TTS know things that the people working on pretraining don't know, and vice versa. Giving them the ability to ship something, like Voxtral, and get feedback from users, is much better than making them wait for the next big multimodal run. Then when we combine, we combine with something that's already been validated.

Eventually, yes, I think everything converges into a single model that handles text, audio, images natively. But I'd rather get there step by step than bet everything on one giant run.

r001.rationale: The response says separate audio training lets the team iterate, ablate, and test audio components, then connect a validated audio model to the language model.

astra-6.text: The idea is to get the audio capabilities right on their own first. When you combine everything from the beginning, it becomes harder to understand where improvements or limitations are coming from. Is it the audio component, the language model, or the way they interact? Developing them separately lets us isolate those questions and iterate more easily. Then we can bring them together once we have a solid foundation.

sol-6.1.text:
We wanted to first understand what it takes to build a really good audio model. If you combine everything from the beginning, it becomes harder to tell where improvements or limitations are coming from. Working on audio separately lets us focus on the data, the training, and the evaluation, and iterate faster.

Then, once that capability is strong, we can bring it together with the language model. The goal is still a unified experience, but we think there’s value in getting the individual components right first.
